limitations: No data on caffeine use, stress levels, and chronotype
Actigraphy has low specificity for detecting wakefulness within sleep periods
Actigraphy is not sensitive to low light levels
Actigraphy is not calibrated for artificial fluorescent lighting
Wrist actigraphy data may not fully represent light levels reaching the retina
Data collection methods do not allow for differentiation between natural daylight and artificial lighting
No analysis of specific wavelengths of light exposure
Did not account for the roles of views from windows (psychological dimension)

final_result.title: Illuminating the Effects of Dynamic Lighting on Student Learning

findings.antecedent: focus lighting (6000K-100fc average maintained) during instruction
findings.mechanism: focus light setting as an instructional technology improved the reading performance by enhancing concentration, focus, motivation and cognition.
findings.source: Abstract, Results and Discussion, ORF section, Figure 4
findings.quote: Focus lighting led to a higher percentage increase in oral reading fluency performance (36%) than did control lighting (17%).

findings.mechanism: possibly attributable to the younger age level of respondents as compared with European studies.
findings.source: Abstract, Results and Discussion, Motivation and Concentration section
findings.quote: No lighting effects were found for motivation or concentration

findings.mechanism: possibly attributable to the younger age level of respondents as compared with European studies. Also, students were unfamiliar with the test, and it is designed for age 9 and above, while participants were closer to 8.
findings.source: Abstract, Results and Discussion, Motivation and Concentration section, Figure 6 note
findings.quote: Repeated measures ANOVA test for the effect of concentration was not significant, F(2, 1.84) = 225.4, mean standard error = 1203.5, p = .08.

stimuli.description: Classrooms with dynamic lighting systems. Focus lighting: 1000 lux, 6500K. Normal lighting: 500 lux, 3500K. Other settings (energy, calm) were also available but focus was the treatment.
stimuli.source: Participants, Method, and Instrumentation, Figures 2 and 3

limitations: Due to the quasi-experimental design where classrooms were randomly assigned, teacher effects could not be controlled.
All students were tested in a normal lighting environment, which may have disadvantaged the focus lighting group due to encoding specificity.
Only one measure was used for each of the three dependent variables, potentially leading to a failure to find differences on some measures.
Students and teachers might have been aware of the study and conformed by exerting more or less effort (threats to internal validity).

final_result.title: Preference for Curvilinear Contour in Interior Architectural Spaces: Evidence From Experts and Nonexperts

findings.mechanism: people appear to associate curvilinear contour with positive and pleasant emotions
findings.quote: significant main effect of contour (b = .847, z = 4.856, p < .001), indicating that there was a significantly higher probability for participants to find curvilinear interior spaces (.65, 95% CI [.59, .70]) beautiful than rectilinear interior spaces (.44, 95% CI [.38, .50]).

significant main effect of expertise (b = -.403, z = 2.311, p = .021), indicating that nonexpert participants were more likely to rate the images as beautiful (.60, 95% CI [.54, .66]) than expert participants (.50, 95% CI [.44, .56]).

findings.mechanism: contour is a more salient variable to architects and designers than it is to nonexpert participants
findings.quote: significant interaction between contour and expertise (b = .870, z = 2.493, p = .013), indicating that the effect of contour was weaker for nonexpert participants than for expert participants (see Figure 1).

findings.antecedent: interior space contour (curvilinear vs. rectilinear) for nonexperts
findings.quote: the difference between nonexpert participants' responses to curvilinear (.65, 95% CI [.57, .72]) and rectilinear (.55, 95% CI [.46, .63]) interior spaces did not differ from each other (b = .412, z = 1.691, p = .091).

findings.antecedent: interior space contour (curvilinear vs. rectilinear) for experts
findings.mechanism: contour is a more salient variable to architects and designers
findings.quote: expert participants regarded as beautiful a significantly greater proportion (b = 1.282; z = 5.134; p < .001) of curvilinear interior spaces (.66, 95% CI [.57, .73]) than rectilinear interior spaces (.35, 95% CI [.27, .43]).

findings.antecedent: task order (beauty first vs. willingness to enter first)
findings.quote: Task order had no effect on participants' responses in the beauty task (b = -.002, z = 0.140, p = .889).

findings.mechanism: affordances of curvilinear contour
findings.quote: significant main effect of contour (b = .461, z = 2.646, p = .008), indicating that participants were significantly more likely to opt to enter curvilinear interior spaces (.66, 95% CI [.60, .71]) than rectilinear interior spaces (.55, 95% CI [.49, .60]).
The main effect of expertise was not significant (b = -.290, z = 1.665, p = .096).

findings.mechanism: Experts may be trained to view images of architectural spaces dispassionately and be less subject to implicit behavioral biases rendered by their visual features
findings.quote: the main effect of contour was qualified by a significant interaction between contour and expertise (b = -.865, z = 2.482, p = .013), indicating that the effect of contour was weaker for expert than for nonexpert participants (see Figure 2).

findings.antecedent: interior space contour (curvilinear vs. rectilinear) for experts
findings.mechanism: Experts may be trained to view images of architectural spaces dispassionately and be less subject to implicit behavioral biases rendered by their visual features
findings.quote: the difference between expert participants' responses to curvilinear (.57, 95% CI [.49, .65]) and rectilinear (.56, 95% CI: .48, .64]) interior spaces was not significant (b = .031, z = 0.126, p = .899).

findings.antecedent: interior space contour (curvilinear vs. rectilinear) for nonexperts
findings.mechanism: affordances of curvilinear contour
findings.quote: nonexpert participants were willing to enter a significantly greater proportion (b = .894, z = 3.529, p < .001) of curvilinear interior spaces (.73, 95% CI [.65, .80]) than rectilinear interior spaces (.53, 95% CI: [.45, .61]).

findings.antecedent: task order (beauty first vs. willingness to enter first)
findings.quote: Task order had no effect on participants' responses to the enter task (b = .004, z = 0.024, p = .981).

stimuli.description: eight images of interior architectural spaces, four curvilinear and four rectilinear, presented in color in a booklet.

limitations: Data collected from a relatively small number of stimuli (8 images).
Used dichotomous scales for beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions, which might limit the granularity of responses.
The context of data collection varied between expert and nonexpert groups.
